content: 1. Among the study participants, 65% were aged 65 to 74 years, while 6% (n = 1,095) were 75 years or older. 2. Women aged 75 years and older demonstrated a higher relative risk of non-fatal stroke and invasive breast cancer when treated with conjugated estrogens plus medroxyprogesterone acetate (CE/MPA) compared to placebo, as opposed to women under 75 years of age. 3. In women over 75 years old, the increased risk of non-fatal stroke and invasive breast cancer in the CE/MPA group compared to the placebo group was 75 versus 24 cases per 10,000 women-years and 52 versus 12 cases per 10,000 women-years, respectively. 4. In the estrogen-plus-progestin sub-study of the Women’s Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS), 4,532 postmenopausal women aged 65 to 79 years were randomized to receive CE/MPA (CE 0.625 mg/MPA 2.5 mg) or placebo. 5. After an average follow-up of 4 years, the relative risk of probable dementia in the CE/MPA group compared to placebo was 2.05 (95% CI 1.21–3.48). 6. The absolute risk of developing probable dementia with CE/MPA was 45 cases per 10,000 women-years compared to 22 cases per 10,000 women-years in the placebo group. 7. Among the cases of probable dementia, 79% occurred in women older than 70 years in the CE group, and 82% occurred in women older than 70 years in the CE/MPA group. 8. Alzheimer’s disease was the most common classification of probable dementia in both the treatment and placebo groups. 9. When data from the two populations were pooled as planned in the WHIMS protocol, the overall relative risk for probable dementia was 1.76 (95% CI 1.19–2.60). 10. Since both sub-studies were conducted in women aged 65 to 79 years, it remains unknown whether these findings are applicable to younger postmenopausal women. 11. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Conjugated Estrogens Synthetic B with respect to specific gender populations, racial populations, renal impairment, hepatic impairment, women of reproductive potential, males, or immunocompromised patients. 12. Conjugated Estrogens Synthetic B is administered orally, and the FDA package insert contains no specific information regarding drug monitoring. 13. Limited information is available regarding the intravenous compatibility of Conjugated Estrogens Synthetic B. 14. Serious adverse effects have not been reported following acute ingestion of large doses of estrogen-containing products by young children. Overdosage of estrogen may cause nausea, vomiting, and withdrawal bleeding in females. 15. Circulating estrogens modulate the pituitary secretion of gonadotropins, luteinizing hormone (LH), and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) through a negative feedback mechanism. Estrogens reduce the elevated levels of these hormones in postmenopausal women. 16. ENJUVIA® tablets contain a blend of ten synthetic estrogenic substances, including sodium estrone sulfate, sodium equilin sulfate, sodium 17α-dihydroequilin sulfate, sodium 17α-estradiol sulfate, sodium 17β-dihydroequilin sulfate, sodium 17α-dihydroequilenin sulfate, sodium 17β-dihydroequilenin sulfate, sodium equilenin sulfate, sodium 17β-estradiol sulfate, and sodium Δ8,9-dehydroestrone sulfate. 17. ENJUVIA tablets are available in strengths of 0.3 mg, 0.45 mg, 0.625 mg, 0.9 mg, and 1.25 mg of synthetic conjugated estrogens, B. 18. The tablets also contain inactive ingredients such as ascorbyl palmitate, butylated hydroxyanisole, colloidal silicon dioxide, edetate disodium dihydrate, plasticized ethyl cellulose, hypromellose, lactose monohydrate, magnesium stearate, purified water, iron oxide red, titanium dioxide, polyethylene glycol, polysorbate 80, triacetate, and triacetin/glycerol. 19. Synthetic conjugated estrogens, B, are water-soluble and well absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract after release from the drug formulation. ENJUVIA tablets release synthetic conjugated estrogens, B, slowly over several hours. 20. The pharmacokinetics of synthetic conjugated estrogens, B, following administration of ENJUVIA tablets under fasting conditions have been studied, but the effect of food on their bioavailability has not been evaluated. However, food did not significantly affect the pharmacokinetics of a similar formulation. 21. Exogenous estrogens are metabolized in the same manner as endogenous estrogens, undergoing metabolic interconversions primarily in the liver. Estradiol is reversibly converted to estrone, and both can be converted to estriol, the major urinary metabolite. 22. Estrogens undergo enterohepatic recirculation via sulfate and glucuronide conjugation in the liver, biliary secretion of conjugates into the intestine, hydrolysis in the intestine, and reabsorption. 23. In postmenopausal women, a significant portion of circulating estrogens exists as sulfate conjugates, particularly estrone sulfate, which serves as a circulating reservoir for the formation of more active estrogens. 24. Estradiol, estrone, and estriol are excreted in the urine along with glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. 25. The mean (SD) apparent terminal elimination half-life (t½) of conjugated estrone is 14 (±6) hours, and conjugated equilin is 11 (±6) hours. 26. No pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in special populations, including patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 27. Long-term continuous administration of natural and synthetic estrogens in certain animal species increases the frequency of carcinomas of the breast, uterus, cervix, vagina, testis, and liver. 28. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging, multi-center clinical study was conducted to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of ENJUVIA tablets for the treatment of vasomotor symptoms in 281 naturally or surgically postmenopausal women.
